成都で働く日本人会社員、二十七歳。中国の家庭に招かれるのは初めて: Japanese office worker in Chengdu, 27. Her first time being invited to a Chinese home.
陈静のお母さん、五十代。料理上手で、お客さんにとにかくたくさん食べさせたい: Chen Jing's mother, in her fifties. A great cook who wants her guests to eat as much as possible.

友達のお母さんは「阿姨」と呼びます。「打扰了」は「おじゃまします」にあたる言葉。: A friend's mother is addressed as 「阿姨」. 「打扰了」 is what you say when entering someone's home, like "sorry to intrude." 「阿姨」 is a respectful, affectionate term, so you can use it with confidence.
おじゃまなんてとんでもない。来るの大変だったでしょう？: Not at all, not at all. Was it a tiring trip over?

If you translate a self-deprecating phrase like "it's nothing much" literally as 「不好的东西」 ("a bad thing"), people will wonder, "Why would you give me something bad?" 中国では贈り物をもらうと、まず「太客气了」「还带什么东西」と一度遠慮するのがお決: In China, when receiving a gift, it's customary to politely protest once with 「太客气了」 or 「还带什么东西」. They're not really refusing, so don't be put off: say 「应该的」 and offer it again.

中国の家庭では、お母さんがお客さんのお皿にどんどん料理を取ってくれます（夹菜）。: In Chinese homes, the mother will keep putting food on the guest's plate (「夹菜」). This is the highest form of hospitality. Even if you can't finish it all, the best manners are to take a bite first and say what you think of the taste.

うちのお母さんっていつもこうなの。お客さんがお腹いっぱいにならないんじゃないかっ: That's just how my mom is. She's always afraid guests won't get enough to eat. Haha.

中国のお母さんにとって、子どもの友達がおいしそうに食べてくれるのは何よりの喜び。: For a Chinese mother, nothing is more delightful than seeing her child's friend enjoy the food. 「多吃点儿」 is an expression of love meaning "I welcome you like family." She'll truly come to love someone who accepts that and praises her cooking.
